blocks.content: Names are one of the most important parts of writing clean code. A good name acts as built-in documentation and helps developers understand code without opening method implementations or reading comments.
Unlike comments, which can become outdated over time, names appear everywhere the code is used. Because of this, names are often the most reliable form of documentation in a codebase.
The goal of naming is simple: A reader should understand what something is, what it does, or what it stores just by reading its name.
1. Style Is Not the Same as Quality
blocks.text: 1. Style Is Not the Same as Quality

blocks.content: Many developers think naming conventions are only about formatting rules such as camelCase, PascalCase, or snake_case. While consistency is important, formatting alone does not make a name meaningful.
Consider these two method names:
processData(data)
calculateDiscountedTotal(order)

Both follow proper naming conventions. However, the first name is vague and provides very little information. The second name clearly explains what the method does before you even read its implementation. This is the difference between a correctly formatted name and a high-quality name.
A good name should answer one of these questions immediately:
["What is this?","What does it do?","What value does it hold?"]
If the reader has to open the implementation to understand the purpose, the name is probably too vague.
2. The Five Qualities of a Genuinely Good Name
blocks.text: 2. The Five Qualities of a Genuinely Good Name

blocks.content: 1. A name is the most important piece of documentation in a codebase

because it is seen every time the code is read, modified, or reviewed. Unlike comments, which can become outdated or be ignored entirely, names remain at every call site and continuously communicate meaning. A well-chosen name reduces cognitive effort and allows developers to understand code without needing additional explanations.
2. The first quality of a good name is that it reveals intent.
A reader should immediately understand why a variable, method, or class exists and what role it plays.
Names such as elapsedTimeInDays or customerAccountBalance provide meaningful context, whereas vague names like d, temp, or value force readers to investigate further before understanding the code.
3. A good name must also avoid disinformation.

Names create expectations, and misleading names create confusion. If a collection is implemented as a hash set, calling it accountList suggests ordering and indexing behavior that does not actually exist. Accurate names build trust, while inaccurate names make code harder to reason about and more prone to misuse.
4. Another essential characteristic is pronounceability and searchability.

Developers discuss code in meetings, code reviews, and debugging sessions, so names should be easy to say aloud. They should also be easy to locate through project-wide searches. Cryptic abbreviations, random acronyms, and single-letter identifiers make communication difficult and often lead to misunderstandings.
5. Good names also match their scope.
The amount of detail a name contains should be proportional to how broadly it is used. A short name like i works well inside a small loop because its purpose is immediately obvious.

However, a public method, shared utility, or domain object may be read by hundreds of developers over many years, and therefore requires a much more descriptive name that can stand on its own without additional context.
6. Finally, good names make code read naturally.
Method names should describe actions, and boolean names should read like questions whose answers are either true or false.

Names such as isValid(), hasPermission(), and canRetry() create code that reads almost like plain English. When names are chosen carefully, the code becomes self-explanatory, reducing the need for comments and making the entire system easier to understand, maintain, and evolve over time.

In the end, naming is not a cosmetic activity it is a design activity. Every good name captures intent, communicates meaning, and makes the next developer's job easier. Clear naming turns complex code into understandable code, and understandable code is the foundation of maintainable software.
3. Per-language formatting conventions
Once the name itself is good, the formatting style is what makes it feel native to the language it's written in.
Mixing styles within one codebase or worse, within one file is its own kind of inconsistency that slows every reader down, even when each individual name is well chosen.
1. Classes and interfaces: UpperCamelCase

class BankAccount { }
interface PaymentGateway { }
2. Methods and variables: lowerCamelCase
3. Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE with static final

static final int MAX_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 3;

static final double DEFAULT_TAX_RATE = 0.08;

5. boolean methods read as yes/no questions

blocks.content: 4. Where the languages genuinely disagree
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781973529339-420683280.png
The single most important thing to notice in that table is the "private signaling" row.
In Java and C++, marking something private is enforced by the compiler code outside the class genuinely cannot access it, no matter what it's named.
In Python, the leading underscore is purely a social convention between the author and anyone reading the code; nothing stops external code from reaching in and usingaccount._balancedirectly.
Treating Python's underscore prefix as real protection, the way Java'sprivatekeyword is real protection, is a common and consequential misunderstanding.
5. What Good Names Look Like

Good names make code easier to understand without reading comments or implementations. Regardless of the programming language, the meaning should stay the same the only thing that changes is the naming style (camelCase, PascalCase, or snake_case).
1. Use Verbs for Actions
Methods and functions perform actions, so their names should be verbs.
Good examples include calculateTotal, validateEmail, and sendNotification.
When someone reads these names, they immediately understand what the function does without opening its implementation.
2. Use Nouns for Things
Classes, objects, and variables represent things, so their names should be nouns.
Examples include BankAccount, Order, customerName, and retryCount.
A noun tells the reader what the object or value represents.
3. Make Units Explicit
Whenever a value has a unit such as time, size, or distance, include the unit in the name.
Names like timeoutMs, timeoutSeconds, and fileSizeMB are much clearer than generic names such as timeout or size.
A clear unit prevents misunderstandings and avoids subtle bugs.
4. Be Consistent
Use the same name for the same concept throughout the codebase.
For example, if you choose userId, use userId everywhere instead of mixing it with names like uid, userID, or customerId.
Consistency reduces mental effort because developers do not have to translate between different names for the same concept.
6. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Encoding the type in the name: Avoid names like accountList, userArray, or customerSet. These names describe the implementation rather than the thing itself. If the underlying data structure changes later, the name becomes misleading.
Prefer names like accounts, users, or customers. The name should describe what the data represents, not how it is stored.
Mistake 2: Using single-letter names outside small scopes
blocks.text: Mistake 2: Using single-letter names outside small scopes

blocks.content: A name like i is acceptable inside a short loop because its meaning is obvious and its scope is very small. Using names like x, d, or u for method parameters, class fields, or large functions makes code harder to understand.
Use descriptive names such as user, distance, or totalAmount so readers immediately know what the value represents.
Mistake 3: Treating Python's underscore as real access control
blocks.text: Mistake 3: Treating Python's underscore as real access control

blocks.content: In Python, a name such as _balance does not make a field private. The underscore is only a convention that tells other developers the field is intended for internal use.
Unlike Java's private keyword, Python does not enforce access restrictions. Other code can still access _balance if it chooses to.
Mistake 4: Naming booleans as nouns
blocks.text: Mistake 4: Naming booleans as nouns

blocks.content: Names like status, flag, or state do not clearly indicate what true or false means. Readers often need to look up the definition to understand them.
Boolean names should read like questions. Names such as isActive, hasExpired, and canRetry make the meaning clear wherever they are used.
7. Quick Reference
Reveal intent: A good name should explain what something is or what it does without requiring the reader to inspect its implementation.
Java naming:

["Classes use UpperCamelCase.

items: Methods and variables use lowerCamelCase.

blocks.content: C++ naming: Classes commonly use UpperCamelCase. Functions often use snake_case. Member fields are frequently written with a trailing underscore.
Python naming: Classes use UpperCamelCase. Functions and variables use snake_case. A leading underscore indicates internal use by convention only.
Booleans as questions: Boolean names should clearly express a condition, such as isValid, hasPermission, or canRetry.

Consistency over cleverness: Use the same name for the same concept throughout the codebase. If something is called user in one place, avoid calling it customer or client elsewhere unless it truly represents a different concept.
